strengths: Addresses a genuine practical limitation of prior unified HSI restoration methods, i.e., reliance on explicit degradation labels/textual prompts that are hard to obtain in real-world settings, and proposes an interpretable, label-free alternative (spatial-spectral metrics) grounded in physically meaningful quantities (HFER, STU, SCM, etc.).

Comprehensive metric selection pipeline (25 candidates -> interpretability/coverage/discriminability filtering -> correlation and Random Forest importance analysis) is methodologically sound and transparently documented in the supplementary material.

Extensive experimental validation across eight datasets spanning both natural-scene and remote-sensing HSI domains, five restoration tasks, and zero-shot generalization to two unseen degradation types (motion deblurring, Poisson denoising), with consistent and often substantial improvements over strong all-in-one and task-specific baselines.

Thorough ablations covering component contribution (DP vs SSAM), routing strategy comparisons, plug-and-play generalization of DP to other architectures (MoCE-IR, MP-HSIR), number/activation of experts, and multi-task vs single-task training, which support the individual design choices.
Efficiency comparison shows competitive FLOPs/parameters/runtime relative to several baselines despite higher restoration quality, and the additional cost of DP itself is shown to be minimal.
Clear figures (t-SNE, confusion matrix, metric distribution plots) provide reasonable evidence that the chosen metrics carry discriminative information about degradation type/severity.
weaknesses: The core novelty relative to prior implicit degradation-aware encoding methods (e.g., degradation-aware encoding/AirNet-style approaches cited as related work [13]) is not clearly differentiated experimentally; no direct baseline comparison against such implicit (non-metric, non-textual) degradation-conditioning methods is provided, making it hard to isolate the specific benefit of hand-crafted metrics versus learned implicit degradation embeddings.

The metrics and their selection (Random Forest importance, correlation filtering) were tuned specifically to discriminate among five synthetic degradation categories (noise, blur, low-resolution, missing regions, band missing); it is unclear whether this metric set truly generalizes to genuinely novel or complex real-world mixed degradations not represented in this taxonomy, somewhat undercutting the claim of eliminating dependence on predefined degradation types.

Despite the abstract's emphasis on handling 'diverse, mixed' degradations, the experiments largely test single-degradation-type tasks (with fixed parameter ranges) rather than genuinely compound/mixed degradations; the zero-shot generalization is also tested only on two additional single-type degradations on one relatively simple dataset (CAVE), not on remote-sensing or truly compound corruptions.

The ablation on number of activated experts (Table 12) shows that top-1 routing (i.e., selecting a single expert) consistently outperforms activating more experts, which suggests the model is effectively learning a near-discrete degradation-type classifier rather than leveraging continuous multi-dimensional degradation information as claimed; this finding is not discussed or reconciled with the paper's central narrative about continuous, multi-dimensional degradation prompting.

Reported FLOPs (~313G) remain an order of magnitude higher than InstructIR (~30G), so claims of 'efficient' restoration are only relative to some heavier baselines (PromptIR, DFPIR, MP-HSIR) and somewhat overstated in the text.

No statistical significance testing, variance/error bars, or repeated-run reporting is provided for the PSNR/SSIM improvements, several of which (e.g., 0.1–0.5dB gains in some tables) are numerically modest.

Only pixel-fidelity metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are reported; no perceptual or downstream-task (e.g., classification) evaluation is included despite motivating the work partly via downstream tasks like classification/change detection in the introduction.

Reproducibility could be improved: while a supplementary section details datasets/settings, some architectural specifics (e.g., exact routing function fproj, training of the router without ground-truth degradation labels, shared vs specialized expert dimension ratios) are only briefly described, and code availability is only promised, not verifiable at review time.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap in unified HSI restoration: reliance on either impractical explicit priors or opaque black-box degradation embeddings. The proposed interpretable spatial-spectral metric representation (DP) is a reasonable and practically useful alternative.

Extensive empirical validation across 8 datasets (natural and remote sensing), 5 unified restoration tasks, and 2 zero-shot tasks, compared against both task-specific and unified SOTA baselines, with consistent state-of-the-art results.

Thorough ablation studies in the supplementary material, including expert count, activated experts, routing noise sensitivity, leave-one-out metric ablation, and comparison of metric-set sizes (3 vs 6 vs 12), which lend credibility to design choices.
Efficiency analysis shows the method achieves competitive or superior FLOPs/parameters/inference time relative to baselines, supporting practical applicability.

Interesting analysis of expert specialization (spatial vs spectral) via learned fusion coefficients, with visualizations showing meaningful, non-trivial correlation between degradation type and expert activation.

Additional robustness checks (spatially heterogeneous degradations, extreme combined degradations, real-world dataset, comparison with unsupervised/self-supervised methods, scalability with spectral bands) substantially strengthen the empirical case.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: combining hand-crafted, interpretable image-quality metrics as a conditioning/gating signal within an MoE architecture is a natural engineering extension of existing prompt-based/MoE restoration methods (e.g., MoCE-IR, PromptIR) rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

The metric selection pipeline (correlation threshold ρ<0.8, RF importance ranking, manual interpretability filtering) involves several heuristic and somewhat arbitrary choices; sensitivity of final results to these choices is not deeply analyzed, raising reproducibility concerns despite the stated interpretability goal.

The claimed monotonic metric-severity relationship is not fully supported: Fig. 7 shows a non-significant correlation (r=0.100, n.s.) for one of the analyzed metric-degradation pairs, and correlation strength varies substantially across degradation types, weakening the universal-representation claim.

Zero-shot generalization is validated on only two unseen degradation types (motion deblurring, Poisson denoising); broader coverage of qualitatively different corruptions (e.g., non-additive, highly structured, or sensor-specific artifacts) would better support the generalization claims made in the abstract/introduction.
Real-world validation is limited to a single small dataset with only 8 test images, which is not sufficient to strongly support claims of real-world applicability.
No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported across runs, despite comparisons involving many closely-spaced PSNR/SSIM values across numerous baselines and datasets.

The constraint that λs/λc are expert-specific (not instance-specific) is an important architectural design choice, but the paper provides limited ablation/justification comparing this against instance-adaptive alternatives beyond a brief qualitative argument.
Code repository link is not filled in within the provided manuscript text, limiting verification of reproducibility during review.

strengths: The core idea of replacing explicit degradation priors/labels or opaque black-box embeddings with a compact, interpretable spatial-spectral metric vector (DP) is a sensible and well-motivated direction for improving generalization in unified HSI restoration.

The SSAM design, which forces individual experts to specialize via fixed, expert-specific learnable spatial/spectral fusion coefficients rather than instance-adaptive coefficients, is a clean and interpretable mechanism for expert disentanglement, and the paper provides supporting visualizations (Fig. 12) showing polarization into spatial- vs. spectral-heavy experts.

The experimental scope is extensive: five in-distribution tasks across natural and remote-sensing datasets, two zero-shot tasks, plus a large number of supplementary studies (extreme/mixed degradations, real-world data, expert activation analysis, routing noise sensitivity, spectral-band scalability).
Efficiency numbers are favorable relative to competing all-in-one baselines (fewer FLOPs/parameters and lower latency while achieving higher PSNR/SSIM).
Ablations on the number of experts, activated experts, and metric leave-one-out are reasonably systematic and support the design choices made.
weaknesses: The derivation of the '6 optimal metrics' is somewhat circular and narrow: metrics are selected via a Random Forest classifier trained to discriminate only the five synthetic degradation categories used in the paper's own experiments (on small pilot sets of 500–1,000 patches). This risks overfitting the metric selection itself to the closed set of degradation types being tested, undermining the central claim that DP generalizes better than black-box representations to genuinely unseen degradation physics.

Some metric definitions/interpretations in Table 1 and Table 7 appear internally inconsistent or under-specified (e.g., 'Spatial Texture Uniformity' is described as 'spectral smoothness measured by geometric-to-arithmetic mean ratio,' and formulas use undefined quantities such as s_i in SCM without clear definition in the main text), raising concerns about the rigor/soundness of the proposed interpretable-metric framework as actually presented.

The claim that interpretable metrics 'fundamentally enhance generalization' compared to black-box latents is asserted narratively (Section 3.2) rather than derived or tested with a controlled ablation isolating interpretability per se from the specific metric choices and MoE architecture changes—the zero-shot gains could equally stem from the MoE/SSAM architecture rather than the interpretability of DP.

Some baseline results look suspiciously fragile in cross-task comparisons (e.g., MP-HSIR's PSNR collapses to 16.96 dB on zero-shot Poisson denoising despite being competitive or SOTA on many in-distribution tasks), suggesting possible reproduction/tuning inconsistencies for baselines that could bias the reported margins in DAMP's favor.

The architectural contribution (MoE with degradation-conditioned routing, combined with attention-based spatial/spectral branches) is largely an incremental combination of existing ideas (MoCE-IR-style MoE, PromptIR-style conditioning, dual spatial/spectral attention already common in HSI restoration); the primary novelty is confined to the hand-engineered metric vector rather than a fundamentally new architectural or theoretical mechanism.

The extensive appendix (Sections E.1–E.10) reads as a large number of favorable post-hoc experiments added seemingly to preempt every possible reviewer concern, all of which uniformly favor the proposed method without any reported negative or mixed result, which is unusual and reduces confidence in the objectivity of the evaluation.
Real-world validation (Section E.10) is very limited—only 8 test images from a single real dataset—insufficient to strongly support claims of practical applicability to genuine unseen degradations.

No variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere, making it hard to assess whether the often small margins over the strongest baselines (e.g., Gaussian deblurring PSNR gains of ~0.2–0.3 dB on ICVL/HyRank, SSIM differences in the third decimal) are statistically meaningful.

strengths: The core idea—replacing explicit degradation labels/text prompts and opaque black-box embeddings with a compact, interpretable 6-dimensional spatial-spectral metric vector (DP)—is a sensible middle ground that is well-motivated by the t-SNE/confusion-matrix/distribution analyses in Fig. 2 and Fig. 7.

The DAMoE + SSAM design is architecturally clean: expert-specific fixed fusion coefficients (λ_s, λ_c) let 'spatial' and 'spectral' experts emerge naturally, and the visualization in Fig. 12/Table 17 shows this specialization empirically without explicit supervision.

Experimental coverage is extensive: 8 datasets spanning natural and remote-sensing HSI, 5 trained tasks plus 2 zero-shot tasks, comparisons against 5 unified and 12 task-specific baselines, and thorough ablations (number/activation of experts, routing strategy, routing noise, metric leave-one-out, metric-set size).

The supplementary material proactively addresses many likely reviewer concerns: spatially heterogeneous/localized degradations, extreme combined degradations, comparisons with fully-supervised task-specific SOTA and with unsupervised/self-supervised HSI restoration methods, spectral-resolution scalability, and a real-world dataset evaluation, which strengthens confidence in generalization claims.

Efficiency analysis (Table 6, Table 19) shows the method is competitive or cheaper than baselines in FLOPs/parameters/latency while achieving higher accuracy, and the DP/router overhead is shown to be negligible.
weaknesses: The metric-selection pipeline (25→16→12→6 metrics) relies on Pearson-correlation pruning and Random-Forest feature importance computed on a pilot set containing only the same five degradation categories (noise, blur, low-resolution, region-missing, band-missing) that are later used for training/testing; this raises a mild circularity concern—the 'interpretable' metrics were tuned to discriminate exactly the degradation families the model is later evaluated on, so claims that DP generalizes to arbitrary 'unseen' degradations are only partially tested (the zero-shot tasks, motion blur and Poisson noise, are still fairly close variants of blur/noise already covered).

Correlation strength between individual metrics and degradation severity is highly inconsistent across degradation types (e.g., Fig. 7 shows SCM r=0.995 for Gaussian noise but only r=0.100 (n.s.) for regions-missing, and r=-0.153 for band-missing HFER), suggesting some of the six chosen metrics may contribute little or even negative signal for certain degradations; the paper does not analyze failure cases where DP might be uninformative or misleading.

No statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for any of the main quantitative results (Tables 2–6), making it hard to judge whether the reported gains (often <1 dB PSNR in several tasks) are robust or within noise.

The framework still requires separate models to be trained for natural-scene versus remote-sensing domains, and the 'no explicit prior' claim is somewhat semantic: the network still must learn, during supervised training with known degradation types, how to map DP values to appropriate expert routing, so it is not fully prior-free—this nuance could be discussed more critically rather than being framed purely as an advantage.

Presentation of the extensive supplementary experiments (Sections E.3–E.10) is compressed into brief paragraphs with single-run numbers and no methodological detail on how e.g. 'spatially mixed' or 'extreme combined' degradations were synthesized beyond one sentence, limiting reproducibility of these auxiliary validations even though they are used to counter major generalization concerns.
